paragraphs.heading: The earliest known civilization
paragraphs.text: Sumer is the oldest civilization we know of. It arose in southern Mesopotamia, now south-central Iraq, between the 5th and 4th millennium BC, during the Chalcolithic and early Bronze Ages. Like nearby Elam, it counts as one of the cradles of civilization, alongside Egypt, the Indus Valley, Mesoamerica, Caral-Supe and the Yellow River's Erligang culture. Its farmers, living along the Tigris and Euphrates valleys, grew more grain and other crops than they needed, and that surplus let them build towns.

paragraphs.heading: Where writing begins
paragraphs.text: The oldest texts known anywhere were found at Uruk and Jemdet Nasr, two Sumerian cities, and are dated between about 3350 and 2500 BC. Before them came a stretch of proto-writing, from about 4000 to 2500 BC. Sumerian written history goes back to the 27th century BC and earlier, but it stays obscure until the Early Dynastic III period, around the 23rd century BC. From then on the language of the records is easier to decipher, so archaeologists can read the inscriptions of the time.

paragraphs.heading: What they called themselves
paragraphs.text: The word Sumer comes from the name the Akkadians gave to the Sumerians. The Akkadians, who spoke an East Semitic language, went on to conquer the city-states of Sumer. In their own inscriptions, the Sumerians named their land Kengir, meaning “Country of the noble lords”, and called their language Emegir.

paragraphs.heading: Where they came from
paragraphs.text: The origins of the Sumerians are debated. Most historians think a West Asian people speaking Sumerian settled the area for good between about 5500 and 3300 BC. Their language was neither Semitic nor Indo-European, and it is a language isolate. Other scholars have pointed to Dilmun, a place thought to be the island of Bahrain, which Sumerian legends call the home city of Sumer’s land. That idea has not been established, though Mesopotamian-style round disks have been found in Bahrain.

paragraphs.heading: The people before them
paragraphs.text: Before the Sumerians, the region was home to a people now called the Ubaidians or Proto-Euphrateans, thought to have grown out of the Samarra culture of northern Mesopotamia. The Sumerians never mention them, but modern scholars assume they were the first civilizing force in Sumer. They drained marshes for farming, built up trade, and started industries such as weaving, leatherwork, metalwork, masonry and pottery.

paragraphs.heading: Cities, temples and rulers
paragraphs.text: Sumerian civilization took shape in the Uruk period, in the 4th millennium BC. By the late 4th millennium, Sumer was split into many independent city-states, marked off from each other by canals and boundary stones. Each city centred on a temple to its own patron god or goddess. It was ruled either by a priestly governor, the ensi, or by a king, the lugal, who was closely bound to the city's religious rites.

paragraphs.heading: Conquest and comeback
paragraphs.text: Over time the Sumerians lost ground to Semitic states from the northwest. Around 2270 BC the Semitic-speaking kings of the Akkadian Empire conquered Sumer, yet Sumerian lived on as a sacred language. Native Sumerian rule returned for about a century under the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2100 to 2000 BC, though Akkadian also stayed in use for a while.

paragraphs.heading: Found again
paragraphs.text: In the early days of modern archaeology, nobody knew the Sumerians had existed. The word Sumer first appeared in print from Jules Oppert, who used it in a lecture on 17 January 1869. The first big excavations followed at Girsu in 1877, at Nippur from 1889 to 1900, and at Shuruppak in 1902–1903.
